traditions.name: Greek tragedy
traditions.description: Verse drama performed at the Athenian festivals of Dionysus by masked actors and a chorus. Thirty-two tragedies and one complete satyr play survive, by Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides.

traditions.name: Greek comedy
traditions.description: Old Comedy (Aristophanes): fantastical, obscene and political; New Comedy (Menander): domestic plots of love, mistaken identity and recognition, the ancestor of European situation comedy.

traditions.name: Roman comedy
traditions.description: Latin adaptations of Greek New Comedy, performed at public games. Plautus wrote boisterous musical farce; Terence a more refined, character-driven comedy.

traditions.name: Roman tragedy
traditions.description: Latin tragedy on Greek myths. Only the plays attributed to Seneca survive complete; their rhetoric, ghosts and violence shaped Renaissance tragedy.

traditions.name: Sanskrit drama
traditions.description: Classical Indian drama (nāṭya) theorised in the Nāṭyaśāstra. Plays mix Sanskrit (spoken by kings and Brahmins) with Prakrits (women and commoners), aim at evoking rasa, and avoid tragic endings.

traditions.name: Medieval Latin drama
traditions.description: Latin drama of the medieval Church and cloister: liturgical plays growing from the Easter trope, music dramas, and the learned plays of Hrotsvitha and Hildegard.

traditions.name: Nanxi (Southern drama)
traditions.description: The earliest mature form of Chinese drama, from the coastal south around Wenzhou; long, loosely structured song-dramas that grew into chuanqi.

traditions.name: Mystery and miracle plays
traditions.description: Vernacular religious drama: biblical cycles staged by guilds on pageant wagons, passion plays and saints' plays, often performed at Corpus Christi.

traditions.name: Yuan zaju
traditions.description: Northern 'variety drama' of the Yuan dynasty: four acts (zhe) of arias sung by a single lead singer, with spoken dialogue. The golden age of Chinese dramatic literature.

traditions.name: Arabic drama
traditions.description: Medieval shadow plays and, from Marun al-Naqqash's Beirut productions of 1847, modern Arabic theatre in Egypt, the Levant, Iraq and the Gulf.

traditions.name: Medieval secular drama
traditions.description: Farces, pastoral jeux and Shrovetide plays: the comic, worldly side of medieval theatre.

traditions.name: Kyōgen
traditions.description: Comic plays performed between noh pieces, mostly anonymous, featuring clever servants (Tarō-kaja), foolish masters and priests.

traditions.name: Noh
traditions.description: Masked musical drama perfected by Kan'ami and Zeami under shogunal patronage: slow, allusive and Buddhist in spirit, often centred on a ghost who relives a moment of passion.

traditions.name: Chuanqi (Ming–Qing)
traditions.description: Long literary dramas of dozens of scenes, typically romances, sung mostly in the Kunshan (kunqu) style. Includes the masterpieces of Tang Xianzu, Hong Sheng and Kong Shangren.

traditions.name: Morality plays and interludes
traditions.description: Allegorical drama in which personified virtues and vices struggle for the soul of Everyman; and the secular interludes that grew from it.

traditions.name: Early Iberian theatre
traditions.description: The first Spanish and Portuguese dramatists — Juan del Encina, Gil Vicente, Torres Naharro — writing eclogues, autos and farces for court and church.

traditions.name: Italian drama
traditions.description: Renaissance learned comedy and pastoral, the improvised commedia dell'arte, Goldoni's reform comedy, and the modern theatre of Pirandello, De Filippo and Fo.

traditions.name: Colonial-era indigenous drama
traditions.description: Drama in or drawing on indigenous languages and traditions under Spanish rule: Quechua drama in the Andes, Nahuatl and mestizo theatre in Mesoamerica.

traditions.name: Central and Eastern European drama
traditions.description: Polish Romantic drama, the Czech, Hungarian, Romanian, South Slavic and Ukrainian traditions, and the post-war absurdist theatre of the Soviet bloc.

traditions.name: Elizabethan and Jacobean
traditions.description: English Renaissance drama, from the Tudor interludes to the closing of the theatres in 1642: the commercial playhouses of Marlowe, Shakespeare, Jonson, Webster and Middleton.

traditions.name: Hebrew drama
traditions.description: Hebrew drama from the Italian Renaissance and the Haskalah to the Israeli stage.

traditions.name: Spanish Golden Age
traditions.description: The comedia nueva of Lope de Vega, Tirso and Calderón: three-act polymetric verse plays on honour, love and faith, written in vast numbers for the corrales of Spain and New Spain; also autos sacramentales.

traditions.name: Dutch and Flemish drama
traditions.description: The Dutch Golden Age stage of Bredero and Vondel and the modern Dutch theatre.

traditions.name: Kabuki
traditions.description: Popular theatre of the Edo townsmen, performed by all-male casts: spectacular staging, stylised acting (aragoto, wagoto), and a repertoire of history plays, domestic dramas and dance pieces.

traditions.name: Canadian drama
traditions.description: Drama in French and English in what is now Canada, from Lescarbot's masque at Port-Royal to modern Québécois, Anglo-Canadian and Indigenous playwriting.

traditions.name: French classical theatre
traditions.description: Drama of the age of Louis XIII and XIV observing the unities and bienséance: the tragedies of Corneille and Racine and the comedies of Molière.

traditions.name: Restoration and Georgian
traditions.description: English drama after the reopening of the theatres: witty comedy of manners, heroic tragedy, ballad opera and sentimental comedy.

traditions.name: Bunraku (ningyō jōruri)
traditions.description: Japanese puppet theatre: large puppets operated by three puppeteers, with a chanter (tayū) and shamisen. Its plays, by Chikamatsu and others, were also adapted for kabuki.

traditions.name: French and francophone drama after 1700
traditions.description: From Marivaux and Beaumarchais through Romantic drama, boulevard farce and symbolism to the existentialists, the absurdists and contemporary writing in French.

traditions.name: Nordic drama
traditions.description: Danish, Norwegian, Swedish, Finnish and Icelandic drama: Holberg's comedies, then the modern breakthrough of Ibsen and Strindberg, and on to Jon Fosse.

traditions.name: German-language drama
traditions.description: From Lessing and Weimar classicism to Büchner, naturalism, expressionism, Brecht's epic theatre and the post-war Swiss, Austrian and German stage.

traditions.name: Russian drama
traditions.description: From Fonvizin and Griboyedov through Gogol, Ostrovsky and Chekhov to Soviet and post-Soviet theatre.

traditions.name: Taʿziyeh
traditions.description: Persian Shi'i passion drama commemorating the martyrdom of Imam Husayn at Karbala, performed in the month of Muharram; texts are mostly anonymous.

traditions.name: American drama
traditions.description: Drama of the United States, from early comedies and melodramas through O'Neill, Williams and Miller to August Wilson and contemporary writing.

traditions.name: Peking opera
traditions.description: Jingju: a synthesis of regional styles that took shape in Beijing after 1790, combining song, speech, mime and acrobatics around stock role types. Much of the repertoire is anonymous and traditional.

traditions.name: Modern Iberian drama
traditions.description: Spanish, Catalan and Portuguese drama after the Golden Age: neoclassicism, Romanticism, the Generation of '98 and '27, and post-war theatre.

traditions.name: Australian and New Zealand drama
traditions.description: Drama of Australia and Aotearoa New Zealand, from the post-war 'new wave' to Indigenous and contemporary theatre.

traditions.name: Modern British drama
traditions.description: Victorian comic opera and the well-made play, Edwardian social drama, the post-1956 'angry' generation, and contemporary British theatre.

traditions.name: Latin American drama
traditions.description: Modern theatre of Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking Latin America: rural realism, the grotesco criollo, political and collective creation.

traditions.name: Modern South Asian drama
traditions.description: Drama in Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Marathi, Kannada, English, Sinhala and other languages: Parsi theatre, Tagore, the post-independence 'theatre of roots' and the Indian New Drama.

traditions.name: Turkish and Azerbaijani drama
traditions.description: Modern drama in Turkish and Azerbaijani, from Akhundzade's comedies and the Tanzimat stage to the Republic.

traditions.name: Irish drama
traditions.description: Irish playwrights at home and in London — Boucicault, Wilde, Shaw — and the national theatre movement of the Abbey (Yeats, Gregory, Synge, O'Casey) through Beckett, Friel and after; in English and Irish.

traditions.name: Musical theatre
traditions.description: Book musicals, revues and their successors on Broadway, in London's West End and beyond: drama told through song, dance and spoken scenes, from operetta and musical comedy to the integrated and concept musical.

traditions.name: Modern Persian drama
traditions.description: Western-influenced Iranian drama, from early satirical comedies to the modernism of Saedi and Beyzaie.

traditions.name: Yiddish theatre
traditions.description: Professional Yiddish theatre, founded by Abraham Goldfaden in Romania in 1876 and flourishing in Eastern Europe and New York.

traditions.name: Modern Japanese drama
traditions.description: Shinpa, shingeki (Western-style realist drama), the post-war avant-garde and contemporary 'quiet theatre'.

traditions.name: Caribbean drama
traditions.description: Drama of the anglophone, francophone, hispanophone and Creole Caribbean, rooted in carnival, folklore and the colonial experience.

traditions.name: Modern Southeast Asian drama
traditions.description: Modern drama in Southeast Asia, including Philippine sarswela and English-language theatre.

traditions.name: Huaju (spoken drama)
traditions.description: Western-style spoken drama, introduced by Chinese students in Tokyo in 1907; a vehicle for social criticism and modernisation.

traditions.name: Modern Korean drama
traditions.description: Spoken drama (singeuk) that emerged in the colonial period, followed by post-war realism and experimental theatre.

traditions.name: Modern African drama
traditions.description: Literary drama of Africa in English, French and African languages, drawing on ritual, masquerade, storytelling and the struggle against colonialism and apartheid.

traditions.name: Rabinal Achí (Maya dance-drama)
traditions.description: K'iche' Maya dance-drama of masks and music performed in Rabinal, Guatemala; the most important surviving pre-Hispanic theatrical work of the Americas.
